sections.title: How well does your assistant know your code?
body: Ask an assistant where something lives and watch what it does: grep, open a file, open another, grep again. Each file costs context, and the picture it builds is whatever it happened to read.
sections.caption: Search, open, guess.

sections.title: A map that opens on modules
body: Real codebases have thousands of symbols and tens of thousands of edges. Draw them all and you get a hairball. Sensei’s code map opens on modules and the bands between them, and you go down a level when you choose: a module’s files, sorted into code, tests and docs, then a file’s symbols with their callers and callees.

sections.title: See what the code hides
body: Lenses on the same map show what reading files won’t.
points: Structure: layers coloured by direction, so a lower layer calling a higher one stands out
Cycles: only the bands inside a cycle, with their members tinted
Hidden coupling: files that keep changing together in commits with no import between them
Complexity: modules tinted by how much of their code is over a complexity threshold, measured with qlty

sections.title: Catch the doc that’s gone stale
body: When a README says to call LoginService.authenticate() and the code has since renamed it, the doc is wrong, and it misleads the next reader and the next assistant alike.
Sensei reads the identifiers your docs mention and checks them against the live code graph. A doc whose names no longer exist is marked drifted or broken, and the count shows where you’ll see it.

sections.title: The right context on the first turn
body: Sensei’s capabilities are tools the assistant can call during a session: search, the graph, your rules, what it has learned. Instead of grepping its way in, the assistant can ask and get back the relevant files, callers, rules and memories.
When Sensei can’t answer, it says so, and the assistant falls back to searching rather than working from an empty answer.

sections.title: Start with the right way of working
body: Before a chunk of work starts, intake reads it on three axes: lifecycle (existing code, or new), intent (a bug, a feature, an exploration) and risk, which comes from the blast radius in the code graph.
From those it recommends a playbook, such as debug-flow or spec-driven, and you confirm. High-risk work always keeps you in the loop; the rigour follows the risk.

takeaway: Know the code before you change it.
takeawaySub: Sensei maps it, checks it, and hands it over.
